title: Intervals
competency: Write sets of real numbers in interval notation and show them on the number line.

keywords.def: The set of all real numbers between two end points, such as [2, 5) or (−∞, 3].
∞ means no end to the right; −∞ means no end to the left. They are not numbers.
Any rational or irrational number. Every point on the number line is a real number.

en.text: An interval is all the real numbers between two end points. A square bracket means the end point is included. A round bracket means it is not. Infinity is not a number, so it always takes a round bracket.

screens.text: List some real numbers between 2 and 6, including 2 but not 6.
screens.ask: Which list fits? Take a guess.
screens.after: Such lists never end. Can you write the whole set with symbols? Read on.

screens.title: Intervals
paras: A real interval is the set of all real numbers between two numbers.
A square bracket [ ] means the end point is included. On the number line it is a filled circle ●.
A round bracket ( ) means the end point is not included. On the number line it is an empty circle ○.
The symbol ∞ (infinity) means no end to the right. −∞ means no end to the left. ∞ and −∞ are not numbers, so they always take round brackets.

screens.title: Intervals and infinity
defs: The set of all real numbers between two end points. [ ] includes an end point; ( ) does not.
∞ means no end to the right and −∞ means no end to the left. Neither is a number.

screens.title: Pick the brackets
screens.why: −1 is included (square bracket); 4 is not (round bracket).

screens.title: Tables 1.1 and 1.2
paras: Each inequality has an interval that means the same set.
table: greater than or equal to a
less than or equal to a

screens.title: Examples (Figure 1.7)
paras: (i) [3, 5) holds every real number from 3 up to, but not including, 5.
(iv) [0, ∞) is 0 and every number to its right.

screens.title: Spot the mistake
opts: ∞ is not a number, so it can never be included
screens.ans: ∞ is not a number, so it can never be included
screens.why: The interval has no right end, so it is written [2, ∞).

screens.title: Match the sets
screens.text: Match each inequality with its interval.
screens.why: ≤ and ≥ give square brackets. < and > give round brackets. ∞ always takes a round bracket.
screens.clue: Look at each end: is the end point included?

screens.title: Fill the end
screens.text: The real numbers greater than 7 form the interval (7, ?).
screens.why: There is no end to the right, so we write ∞ with a round bracket.
screens.clue: The numbers go on to the right with no end.

screens.title: A club in Mekelle
screens.text: A school club in Mekelle accepts students aged 14 or older, but younger than 18.
screens.ask: Which interval shows the allowed ages x?
screens.clue: Write it as an inequality first. Which end can x equal?
screens.worked: '14 or older' gives 14 ≤ x. 'Younger than 18' gives x < 18. So 14 ≤ x < 18, which is [14, 18).

items.ask: Real numbers between −3 and 8, including both: ___
items.why: Both end points are included, so both brackets are square.
items.clue: Included end points take square brackets.

items.ask: Real numbers between 4 and 6, not including either: ___
items.why: Neither end point is included, so both brackets are round.
items.clue: Ends not included take round brackets.

items.ask: Real numbers to the right of −1, including −1: ___
items.why: −1 is included; there is no right end, so ∞ with a round bracket.
items.clue: What goes at the right end when there is no end?

items.text: How is [1, 3) shown on the number line?
items.clue: Square bracket: filled circle. Round bracket: empty circle.

items.text: How is (−∞, −5] shown on the number line?
items.why: −5 is included, and −∞ means no end to the left.

items.text: How is (−2, 4) ∪ [5, ∞) shown on the number line?
opts: ○ at −2 and 4 with the part between shaded, then ● at 5 shaded to the right
● at −2 and 4 with the part between shaded, then ○ at 5 shaded to the right
○ at −2, shaded all the way to the right
○ at −2 and 4 with the part between shaded, then ○ at 5 shaded to the left
items.ans: ○ at −2 and 4 with the part between shaded, then ● at 5 shaded to the right
items.why: (−2, 4) leaves out both ends; [5, ∞) includes 5 and goes on to the right.
items.clue: Draw each part separately, then put them together.

test.why: Less than or equal to 6: no left end, 6 included.

screens.title: Read the symbols
steps: x < 4 means x is less than 4. x cannot be 4.
x ≤ 4 means x is less than or equal to 4. x can be 4.
x > 4 means x is greater than 4. x cannot be 4.
x ≥ 4 means x is greater than or equal to 4. x can be 4.
−1 ≤ x < 4 means x is at least −1 and less than 4.

screens.title: Your turn
screens.text: Which value of x fits −1 ≤ x < 4?
screens.why: ≤ allows x to equal −1. The < at 4 does not allow 4.
screens.clue: Which end has the 'or equal to' line under it?
